opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I have pretty mixed feelings about. On the one hand, I think it's a really healthy development. For a long time, the field was organized around these fairly narrow tasks: parsing, named entity recognition, summarization on a particular news dataset. We'd all compete to push the number up by half a point. Those benchmarks were useful, they gave us a shared language and made progress measurable, but they also drifted pretty far from what people actually want language systems to do. Once models got good enough that you could just talk to them, it became obvious that the interesting questions were about open-ended interaction: can the system follow instructions, help someone with a real problem, recover when it misunderstands?

On the other hand, as a researcher, it makes me a bit nervous, because evaluation gets so much harder. With the old tasks you had a test set and a metric, and even if the metric was flawed, everybody agreed on what it was. With conversational benchmarks, you're often relying on human preferences, or increasingly on another model acting as a judge. That introduces all sorts of issues: bias toward longer or more confident answers, sensitivity to style over substance, and the fact that the benchmarks themselves can leak into training data really quickly. We're sort of measuring vibes at scale, which is useful, but it's not the same as a rigorous scientific measurement.

There's also an academic angle I think about a lot. The standard tasks were things a grad student could work on with a modest compute budget and make a real contribution. The more the field's notion of progress is defined by "how does this feel in a chat interface," the more that progress gets concentrated in the places that can train and deploy huge models. So part of what I'd like to see is the community building realistic benchmarks that are still careful and reproducible. They should capture the messiness of real use, but they should also have clear, checkable outcomes. Things like coding tasks with tests, or agentic tasks where you can verify whether the goal was achieved, are a nice middle ground.

So overall I'd say it's the right direction, and probably an inevitable one, but we haven't really figured out the science of evaluation for it yet. I think that's one of the most important open problems right now, and honestly one where academics can contribute a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says that conversational benchmarks make evaluation “so much harder” than the old tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's broadly a healthy move, but I'd push back a little on framing it as a clean shift from one thing to another.

For a long time, NLP ran on a pretty specific loop: you have a dataset, a fixed test set, a single number, and progress means moving that number. GLUE, SQuAD, WMT, Penn Treebank parsing before that. The virtue of that setup was that it was honest in a narrow way. Everyone was measured the same way, you could reproduce someone's result, and when a method worked you knew what it worked on. The vice was that the tasks stopped resembling anything anyone actually wanted. Nobody wakes up wanting to label entailment pairs.

What changed is that models got good enough that the interesting failures moved. The failures aren't "can it parse this sentence" anymore, they're "does it follow a long instruction, does it stay coherent over twenty turns, does it know when to say it doesn't know." So the benchmarks moved toward chat-style and open-ended evaluation because that's where the signal is now. That part I think is just correct. If you keep evaluating on the old tasks, you saturate them and learn nothing.

The thing I worry about is what we gave up. Conversational benchmarks are much harder to score. Often the judge is another model, or it's human preference, and both of those have their own biases. Models that are verbose and confident tend to win preference comparisons, and you can end up optimizing for a style rather than a capability. We also lost some of the reproducibility. When the eval is a leaderboard of pairwise votes, or a closed model grading an open one, it's hard to go back a year later and know exactly what was measured.

So my assessment is something like: the direction is right, the rigor hasn't caught up. The best work I see now tries to have it both ways, realistic tasks that still have some verifiable ground truth. Code is the obvious example, because you can run the tests. Math to some extent. Agentic tasks where there's an actual end state you can check. I'd like to see more of that in language proper, and less reliance on "a model said it was good."

And honestly, as someone who came up on the old task-centric view, I think the field should keep a few of those narrow, boring benchmarks around. Not because they tell you if a model is useful, but because they're the thermometer that still works when everything else is a vibe.

r001.rationale: The response says conversational benchmarks are “much harder to score” and explains that model or human judges introduce bias and reduce reproducibility, making model quality harder to assess.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s exciting, but it makes evaluation much harder. One nice thing about the standard NLP setup was that you could isolate a problem and ask whether you were making progress on it. That didn’t necessarily mean you were solving the thing people actually cared about, but it gave you a fairly clear experimental setup.

With conversation, you’re getting closer to how people want to use these systems. But now there are many reasonable responses, and what counts as a good response depends on the user and on how the conversation develops. So you can gain realism while losing some clarity about what a benchmark score actually tells you.

I’d like to see both: evaluations of whether a system helps someone accomplish a real task, and more controlled tests that let us understand why it succeeds or fails. I don’t think a conversational interface, by itself, solves the gap between a benchmark and real use.

r001.rationale: The candidate says conversational evaluation makes assessment “much harder,” and explains that responses vary by user and conversation context.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a healthy direction. A lot of the standard NLP tasks were useful because they let us isolate a problem and measure progress. But we sometimes ended up treating the benchmark as the problem itself. Getting a higher score on a reading comprehension dataset doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve built something that can help a person understand a document.

Conversation brings some of those missing pieces back in. People are ambiguous, they change what they want, and a good system may need to ask a question rather than immediately produce an answer. Those are interesting capabilities that a single input-output example doesn’t capture very well.

The challenge is that realism makes evaluation harder. If there are many reasonable responses, what exactly are we measuring? Are we rewarding correctness, usefulness, or just an answer that sounds convincing? So I’m excited about moving toward more realistic settings, but I still want evaluations that let us understand why a system succeeds or fails. Ideally, we keep the clarity of the older tasks while broadening what we ask systems to do.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that realism makes evaluation harder and explains that many reasonable responses make it unclear what to measure.
